notes:
# Exodus 22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## v. 1: Theft of Livestock — Fivefold and Fourfold Restitution

**Traditional reading:** This verse applies the eighth commandment (Ex 20:15) to specific cases for judges. The thief who has stolen an ox or sheep and either slaughtered or sold it shows deliberate, calculated intent — he cannot claim he merely "found" or accidentally took the animal. The higher penalty for an ox (fivefold) vs. a sheep (fourfold) is explained in several ways: (a) the ox was the means of a man's livelihood — trained for ploughing, harder to replace, and took years to train; (b) oxen were harder to guard since they grazed scattered, making theft easier and thus requiring a stronger deterrent; (c) the ox was more valuable. Restitution was restorative, not merely punitive — the victim was compensated and the thief impoverished rather than enriched.

- **Gill:** "Five for oxen, because the theft of them hindered from ploughing… and for sheep but four, because there was trouble in the theft of them, and there was no tillage or agriculture by them." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm)
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** Cites Kaiser: "The reason for the fivefold penalty in the case of stealing an ox is probably because one man stole the means of another man's livelihood." Notes that jail was not the Mosaic penalty; restitution plus penalty was required, ranging from 200% to 500%. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)
- **Ligon Duncan (via Precept Austin):** "The law says that theft should result in the enrichment of the victim and the impoverishment of the thief. The law is designed to exactly counteract the intention of the thief's crime." [preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary)
- **Ellicott:** The penalty is heavier when there has been "conversion of the property" — return of fourfold for a sheep, fivefold for an ox. [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "There is a moral fitness in this, since a man's desire to get what was his neighbour's would lead to the loss of what was his own." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)

---

## v. 2: Night-time Burglar Killed — No Bloodguilt

**Traditional reading:** If a thief is caught breaking in (literally "digging through" — since ancient walls were earthen) at night and is struck dead, the homeowner bears no guilt. The assumption is that at night a homeowner cannot know the intruder's intentions (theft only or murder), cannot easily identify him, and cannot summon help. The burglar is considered to have forfeited his right to life by his action.

- **Ellicott:** "Most codes agree with the Mosaic in allowing the inmates of the house to resist such an attempt if made at night, and to shed the blood of the burglar, if necessary. He may be considered as having dissolved the 'social compact'… A murderous intent on his part may be suspected." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm)
- **Gill:** "To kill a man when breaking into a house, and, by all appearance, with an intention to commit murder, if resisted, in defence of a man's self, his life and property, was not to be reckoned murder." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "The principle here laid down has had the sanction of Solon, of the Roman law, and of the law of England. It rests upon the probability that those who break into a house by night bare a murderous intent." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **Precept Austin (Duncan):** "The owner couldn't know. It could have been someone breaking in to do harm to his family and, in that case, life takes precedence." [preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary)

---

## v. 3: Daylight Killing — Bloodguilt; Thief Sold if Unable to Pay

**Traditional reading:** If the break-in occurs after sunrise, killing the thief incurs bloodguilt. In daylight the homeowner can identify the intruder, assess the threat, and call for help. Even thieves retained rights under God's law. Restitution was required; if the thief owned nothing, he was sold into servitude (presumably for up to six years as per Exodus 21:2), with the sale price going to the victim.

- **Gill:** "Coming at broad daylight, and when the sun was up, it was a plain case he came not with a design to murder, but only to steal; besides… the master of the house could call for help and assistance." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm)
- **Ellicott:** "In the daytime no violence is to be feared. The housebreaker seeks to avoid observation, and decamps if discovered. Moreover, assistance is readily obtainable, and thus there is no need of resorting to extreme measures." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm)
- **Precept Austin (Bruckner):** Notes that the Code of Hammurabi §8 called for execution of a thief who could not pay and inflicted heavier fines; "Hebrew law never imposed death for violation against property." [preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary)
- **David Guzik:** "It is typical of Israel's merciful law that even a thief has his rights." (citing Cole) [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)

---

## v. 4: Stolen Animal Found Alive — Double Restitution

**Traditional reading:** If the stolen animal is found alive in the thief's possession (not slaughtered or sold), the penalty is double, not fourfold or fivefold. The lesser penalty reflects that the owner suffers less loss (the animal is returned alive) and the thief has shown less hardened intent. The principle of restitution still applies — simply returning the animal is not enough; penalty is added.

- **Gill:** "The reason why here only a double restitution and not fourfold is insisted on… is because there the theft is persisted in, here not." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Double restitution was a sort of 'retaliation' — it involved a man losing the exact amount which he had expected to gain." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **Precept Austin (Rayburn):** "He must be punished for what he did and it is no punishment simply to make him give back what he stole. He must suffer some positive loss." [preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary)

---

## v. 5: Livestock Grazing in Another's Field — Restitution from the Best

**Traditional reading:** If a man deliberately allows his animals to graze in another's field or vineyard, he must compensate from the best of his own produce. This goes beyond simple compensation — the law requires restitution from the offender's best, not his worst, ensuring the punishment is genuinely felt. The passage covers willful negligence, not mere accident.

- **Ellicott:** "Voluntary injury… was to be more than compensated. The amount of produce destroyed was to be exactly calculated, and then the injurer was to make good the full amount of his neighbour's loss out of the best of his own produce." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm)
- **David Guzik (citing Morgan):** "These laws also began by laying emphasis on the guilt of carelessness. The truth emphasized is that no man must live his life on the basis of selfishness or wholly alone and that wrong inflicted on neighbour by neighbour in the material realm becomes sin against God in the moral realm." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Without reference to the quality of the crop damaged, the injurer should forfeit an equal amount of his own best produce." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **F.B. Meyer (via Precept Austin):** "We try to make amends for injury done to another by an extraordinary amount of civility; but we are reluctant in so many words to frankly confess that we have done wrong, and make proper reparation." [preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary)

---

## v. 6: Fire Spreading to Another's Field — Full Restitution

**Traditional reading:** Even if a fire starts accidentally on one's own land, if through negligence it spreads (via thornbushes) and consumes a neighbour's stacked grain, standing grain, or field, the one who started the fire must make full restitution. The principle is that negligence that harms another's property is culpable.

- **Gill:** "Though he kindles the fire upon his own ground, yet being careless of it… for his carelessness in not looking after the fire he had kindled in his own field, he was to make good all the damages." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Notes that burning weeds in dry Eastern lands carried constant danger of fire spreading, requiring careful watch. Neglect of this watch incurred liability. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **David Guzik:** "A Christian, if he backs into someone else's car, will certainly leave a note and make good the damage." This extends the principle to modern life. [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)

---

## vv. 7–8: Goods Entrusted for Safekeeping — Thief Pays Double; Otherwise Judges Decide

**Traditional reading:** If someone deposits money or goods with a neighbour and they are stolen, the thief (if caught) pays double. If the thief is not found, the homeowner must appear before the judges (here called *Elohim* — "gods," meaning the magistrates as God's representatives) to determine whether he himself embezzled the goods. The law protects both the depositor from loss and the trustee from false accusation.

- **Gill:** Notes that this applies to a deposit kept without reward (gratuitous). The owner of the house appears before the judges "to see whether he has put his hand to his neighbour's goods: took them to himself, made use of them, or disposed of them to his own advantage." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm)
- **Ellicott:** "Property deposited in the hands of another for safe keeping might be so easily embezzled by the trustee, or lost through his negligence, that some special laws were needed for its protection." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Notes uncertainty about whether the trustee had to compensate if the thief was not found — Kalisch thought the oath-procedure of v.10 applied. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)

---

## v. 9: Disputed Ownership — Judges Decide; Guilty Party Pays Double

**Traditional reading:** In any case where ownership is disputed — whether ox, donkey, sheep, garment, or lost property — both parties come before the judges. The one found to be in the wrong (whether the accused falsely claiming ownership, or the accuser bringing a false charge) must pay double to the other. This penalises both theft and false accusation.

- **Gill:** "The cause of both parties shall come before the judges; who were to hear what each party had to say, and to examine the witnesses each of them brought… and whom the judges shall condemn… he shall pay double unto his neighbour." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm)
- **David Guzik (citing Cole):** "The Israelites apparently did not follow the Anglo-Saxon dictum of 'finders are keepers': a lost object remains the possession of the original owner, who can claim it on sight." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)
- **Ellicott:** "Embezzlement it punished by requiring the trustee guilty of it to 'pay double.'" [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm)

---

## vv. 10–11: Animal Entrusted Dies or Is Injured — Oath Before the LORD Settles It

**Traditional reading:** If an animal given into a neighbour's care dies, is injured, or is driven away with no witnesses, the neighbour may take an oath before the LORD that he did not lay hands on the property. The owner must accept the oath and demand no restitution. This establishes a presumption of innocence — the accused's sworn testimony stands unless contrary evidence exists.

- **Gill:** "This is called 'the oath of the Lord'… because sworn by him, or in his name, and made before him, in his presence, who is hereby appealed unto." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm)
- **David Guzik:** "This principle is the foundation of our idea that a man is innocent until proven guilty. In this case, the man's oath was taken as true unless proof to the contrary could be found." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)
- **Ellicott:** "In doubtful cases it allowed the trustee to clear himself by an oath." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm)

---

## v. 12: If the Animal Was Stolen — Restitution Required

**Traditional reading:** If the animal was certainly stolen (not merely missing under ambiguous circumstances), the trustee must make restitution. The assumption is that theft could have been prevented by proper care, whereas death by natural causes or wild beasts could not.

- **Ellicott:** "It seems to have been considered that theft could have been prevented by proper care, but that hurts from wild beasts or accidents were not preventible." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm)
- **Gill:** "There was ground for suspicion of fraud; however, there was apparent carelessness." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm)

---

## v. 13: Animal Torn by Beasts — Bring the Carcass as Evidence; No Restitution

**Traditional reading:** If the animal was killed by a wild beast, the trustee brings the torn carcass as evidence and is excused from payment. The physical remains prove what happened and exonerate the caretaker.

- **David Guzik (citing Cole):** "Production of the carcase would show that, while the shepherd could not prevent the kill, he was alert enough to stop the devouring of the prey." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)
- **Ellicott:** "In clear cases to give proof that the loss had happened through unavoidable accident." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm)

---

## vv. 14–15: Borrowed Animal Injured or Dies — Full Restitution Unless Owner Present or Animal Rented

**Traditional reading:** If a man borrows an animal and it is injured or dies while the owner is not present, the borrower must make full restitution (regardless of how it happened). If the owner was present (and thus able to supervise), no restitution is required. If the animal was hired (rented), the hire fee is deemed to cover the risk of loss — no further restitution.

- **Ellicott:** "Lending is a species of deposit; but for the benefit, not of the depositor, but of the man with whom the deposit is made. The obligation of the latter to keep intact and to return is therefore even more stringent." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "If anything were paid for the use of the thing, then it was not borrowed, but hired; and the owner was considered to have counted in the risk of loss or damage in fixing the amount of the hire." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **David Guzik:** "Distinctions were to be made according to fairness and justice, not simply to reward whoever suffered loss. Sometimes loss is suffered, and no one is to blame." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)

---

## vv. 16–17: Seduction of an Unbetrothed Virgin — Pay Dowry, Marry Her, or Pay Bride-Price Anyway

**Traditional reading:** If a man seduces (entices, persuades) a virgin not pledged in marriage and sleeps with her, he must pay the bride-price (dowry) and marry her. If the father absolutely refuses to give her to him (perhaps because the man is unsuitable), the man must still pay the full bride-price of a virgin. This law strongly discouraged premarital sex by attaching serious lifelong financial and marital consequences, and protected the woman's future by ensuring she was not economically ruined by the loss of her virginity.

- **David Guzik:** "This law emphasized the principle that there is no such thing as casual sex… It is to the great detriment of society and culture when the government works against the value of virginity." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "In the East a man commonly pays money, or money's worth, to the parents in order to obtain a wife. The seducer was to comply with this custom… If the father consented, he was compelled to marry the girl, and he was forbidden to repudiate her afterwards." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **David Guzik (citing Clarke):** "This was an exceedingly wise and humane law, and must have operated powerfully against seduction and fornication; because the person who might feel inclined to take the advantage of a young woman knew that he must marry her, and give her a dowry." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)

---

## v. 18: Sorceress — Must Not Be Permitted to Live

**Traditional reading (shared broadly by conservative Protestants):** Sorcery (witchcraft, magic arts) was a capital crime in Israel because it involved trafficking with dark spiritual powers in rebellion against God, renouncing dependence on God in favour of the demonic, and was destructive to the covenant community. The feminine form ("sorceress") is used because women were particularly involved in these practices, but the prohibition covers both sexes (Deut 18:10–11). The Septuagint translates the term as *pharmakos* ("poisoner"), linking sorcery with drug use.

- **Gill:** "Such that had familiar spirits, and conversed with them… deceivers of the people, and leading them into unwarrantable practices, and off of a dependence on God and his providence." [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm)
- **Calvin (via StudyLight):** "Since such illusions carry with them a wicked renunciation of God, no wonder that He would have them punished with death." [studylight.org/commentary/exodus/22-18.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/22-18.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Witchcraft was professedly a league with powers in rebellion against God… an absolute renunciation of religion, and of the authority of Jehovah." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **David Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** "The law shows that such communication [with dark powers] is possible, and the penalty shows that it is dangerous… It is clearly against the will of God that in this life men should hold any communication with the spirit world, save that of direct fellowship with Himself, through His Son, by the Holy Spirit." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)

**Denominational differences on application today:**
- **Reformed (John Piper, Desiring God):** The Old Testament death penalty for sorcery was part of God's theocratic "lesson book for the nations" to show the seriousness of sin. In the New Covenant era, the church does not execute sinners but calls them to repentance. "The sins are just as serious now… The same standards of holiness prevail today as in those days, but we live in a day of mercy, a day of reprieve, a day of salvation and reconciliation with God." Sorcery remains sin but the church's response is excommunication and gospel call, not execution. [desiringgod.org/interviews/why-is-witchcraft-handled-so-differently-across-scripture](https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/why-is-witchcraft-handled-so-differently-across-scripture)
- **Lutheran:** The StudyLight.org commentator listing for this verse includes a Lutheran perspective, but no distinctively Lutheran interpretation was retrieved in the search.
- **General evangelical (David Guzik / Enduring Word):** Notes that "Witchcraft is equally condemned in New Testament days (Acts 13:10; 19:19), but… there is no hint in the New Testament that mediums or witches should be put to death." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)
- **Historical misuse:** The StudyLight.org page notes that the Salem witch trials represented "gross ignorance" of the distinction between the Old and New Covenants: "Many of the instructions in the O.T. have utterly nothing to do with Christianity, and this commandment regarding witches is surely one of them." [studylight.org/commentary/exodus/22-18.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/22-18.html)

---

## v. 19: Bestiality — Death Penalty

**Traditional reading:** Sexual intercourse with an animal was a capital crime. This was practiced among the Canaanites and featured in Canaanite religious myths (the "Tales of Baal"), likely giving it religious significance. It was an "obvious perversion" that defiled the image of God in humanity.

- **David Guzik (citing Cole):** "Bestiality was not only an obvious perversion: it figured so often in the Canaanite cycle 'Tales of Baal' that it probably had a religious significance for the Canaanites." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "The abomination here mentioned is said to have prevailed in Egypt, and even to have formed part of the Egyptian religion." Noted that Greek and Roman legislators did not make it a crime despite regarding it as disgusting. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **Precept Austin (Constable):** "Having intercourse with animals (bestiality) was something the Canaanites and Mesopotamians attributed to their gods and which they practiced in worshipping those gods." [preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary) *(referencing Constable's notes on StudyLight)*

---

## v. 20: Sacrificing to Other Gods — Set Apart for Destruction (*Herem*)

**Traditional reading:** Anyone sacrificing to any god other than the LORD alone was to be "utterly destroyed" — the Hebrew *herem* meaning devoted to destruction, banned from the earth. Sacrifice was the chief act of worship; to sacrifice to another god was to renounce the LORD entirely. Under the theocracy this constituted rebellion and treason against the Divine King.

- **David Guzik:** "This law was often broken, and this penalty was rarely applied. One rare example of its application was when Elijah executed the prophets of Baal in 1 Kings 18:40." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Under a theocracy this was rebellion, and rightly punished with temporal death. In ordinary states it would be no civil offence, and would be left to the final judgment of the Almighty." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **David Guzik (citing Kaiser):** "*Herem* is something devoted to God; however, it is not a voluntary but an involuntary dedication. It is now set apart to be banned from the earth." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)

---

## v. 21: Do Not Exploit or Oppress a Foreign Resident

**Traditional reading:** Israel was forbidden to mistreat or oppress the *ger* (foreign resident, sojourner). The motivation is explicitly redemptive-historical: "for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt." Their own experience of oppression should produce empathy, not cruelty. This law was remarkably humane for the ancient Near East.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "It may be doubted whether such a law as this was ever made in any other country. Foreigners are generally looked upon as 'fair game'… The Mosaic legislation protested strongly against this practice." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **David Guzik:** "A good measure of our moral character is found in how we treat a stranger… He also notes that God's command for kindness toward strangers does not negate a government's right to control borders — Israel only entered Egypt at Pharaoh's express invitation (Gen 47:5–6)." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)
- **Ellicott:** Notes that this law is juxtaposed with three capital crimes, "seems intended to indicate that oppression is among the sins which are most hateful in God's sight." [biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/22.htm)

---

## vv. 22–24: Protection of Widows and Orphans — God Hears Their Cry

**Traditional reading:** Widows and orphans were the most vulnerable in ancient society — without economic provision or legal protection. God explicitly forbids their mistreatment and promises direct divine intervention: He will hear their cry, His anger will be kindled, and He will kill the oppressor with the sword, making *his* wife a widow and *his* children fatherless. This is a *lex talionis* (eye-for-eye) applied by God Himself — the punishment fits the crime.

- **David Guzik:** "The widow and fatherless child were the weakest and most vulnerable members of society. In an unrestrained, survival-of-the-fittest society, they would be the first to suffer abuse." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Notes that the prophets later "denounce this backsliding in the strongest terms" when Israel neglected these laws, and that the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem was in part judgment for this very sin (Jer 22:3–5). [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **Precept Austin (citing Kaiser):** "It was the prophets who chided Israel for their neglect in this area of oppressing the poor and the weak." [preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary)

---

## vv. 25–27: Lending to the Poor — No Interest; Return the Cloak by Sunset

**Traditional reading:** Loans to fellow Israelites who were poor must be interest-free — the lender must not act as a creditor (pressing for repayment harshly). If a poor man's cloak is taken as collateral (pledge), it must be returned by sunset because it served as his only covering and blanket at night. God explicitly states His motive: "for I am compassionate." The poor man's cry reaches God's ears just as the widow's and orphan's do.

- **Gill:** Not retrieved in detail, but the traditional Jewish/Christian reading is that usury between Israelites was forbidden because loans to the poor were to be charitable, not profit-making.
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "It is peculiar to the Jewish law to forbid the lending of money at interest by citizen to citizen… On the other hand, it was distinctly declared (Deut 23:20) that interest might be taken from strangers." ## v. 28: Do Not Blaspheme God or Curse the Ruler of Your People

**Traditional reading:** Two prohibitions in one verse: (1) Do not revile/blaspheme God (*Elohim*); (2) do not curse a ruler (*nasi* — "one exalted among the people," a tribal head or prince). Both God and the authorities He appoints are to be treated with reverence. The Pulpit Commentary specifically argues against translating *Elohim* as "judges" here, insisting it refers to God Himself (since *Elohim* as "judges" always takes the article, which is absent here).

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "The passage must therefore be understood as forbidding men to speak evil of God." The Septuagint and KJV render it "the gods" (i.e., false gods), but the Pulpit rejects this because "the most religious Jews, prophets and others, [spoke] with contempt and contumely of the false gods." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **David Guzik:** Includes this under "Laws regarding holiness and separation unto God." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)

## vv. 29–30: Offerings of Firstfruits and Firstborn — Not Delayed

**Traditional reading:** Israel must not hold back offerings from their harvest (grain and wine). The firstborn of their sons (who were to be redeemed by a payment — Ex 13:13; Num 3:46–48), and the firstborn of cattle and sheep belong to the LORD. For livestock, the firstborn stays with its mother seven days and is offered on the eighth day. This parallels circumcision (eighth day) and reflects the principle that the first and best belong to God. "You must not hold back" implies the temptation to delay or withhold these offerings.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "The phrase, 'thou shalt not delay,' implies that there would be reluctance to comply with this obligation, and that the offering would be continually put off. In Nehemiah's time the entire custom had at one period fallen into disuse." [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **Gill (summary):** "Concerning the offering of firstfruits to God" — the firstborn of sons and cattle, and firstfruits of produce. [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/22.htm)

## v. 31: Holy People — Do Not Eat Meat from a Mauled Animal

**Traditional reading:** Israel is to be a holy people set apart to God. As a concrete expression of this, they must not eat the flesh of an animal torn (mauled) by wild beasts found in the field; it is to be thrown to the dogs. The rationale: such meat (a) would not be properly drained of blood (violating the prohibition against consuming blood), (b) the carnivorous beast that tore it was unclean and imparted uncleanness by contact, and (c) eating it would blur the distinction between Israel and the scavenging animals.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "The blood of such an animal would not be properly drained from it. Some would remain in the tissues, and thence the animal would be unclean; again, the carnivorous beast which 'tore' it would also be unclean, and by contact would impart of its uncleanness." Notes that Deuteronomy 14:21 permitted giving or selling it to a foreigner. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-22.html)
- **David Guzik:** Brief note under "Laws regarding holiness and separation unto God." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)

## Broader Themes Across Exodus 22

**Restitution over incarceration (noted across traditions):** The Mosaic Law consistently required wrongdoers to make restitution rather than be imprisoned. As David Guzik (charismatic/evangelical) puts it: "This can be regarded as a positive approach to the punishment of criminals, putting them to productive restitution and compensating the victims of their theft. These principles are often ignored in the modern administration of justice." [enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-22/)

**Life more valuable than property (noted by Reformed and evangelical sources):** Ligon Duncan (Reformed/Presbyterian) emphasises that the daytime limitation on killing a thief shows "life is more valuable than property." [preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-22-commentary)

**God's special concern for the vulnerable (uniform across traditions):** The laws protecting foreigners, widows, orphans, and the poor, backed by God's direct promise to hear their cry, demonstrate God's character as compassionate defender of the weak. This is a theme uniformly emphasised across Reformed, charismatic, Methodist, and Baptist commentators.
